post:2026-10-09.text:
A product can look finished while its most important decision is still unresolved.

The homepage says who it is for. The onboarding asks for information. The dashboard presents a set of actions. Somewhere between those screens, the user has to understand what to do next and why it is worth doing.

That is the part of design I want to talk about more here.

My background spans product design, creative direction, brand strategy, and startup founding. I’m interested in how those disciplines inform the decisions an early team makes.

For a product review, I would start with one task: follow a new user from the first promise to the first useful outcome. Write down every point where the next step needs an explanation. Then ask which of those explanations belongs in the experience itself.

It is a practical starting point for a conversation between a founder and a designer. It gives us something specific to examine before deciding what to redesign.

Where does a new user need the most help understanding your product today?

post:2026-10-13.text:
If your brand says "simple", try creating an account in your own product.

Notice the things a new customer has to work out. Why do you need this information? What happens after clicking continue? Can they change that choice later?

Each unanswered question adds a bit of work. A shorter form won't help much if people still don't understand what they're signing up for.

I'd take one word from the brand strategy and review the product against it. For "trusted", that might mean showing the price before asking for payment details. For "clear", it might mean saying exactly what a button will do.

My work spans brand strategy and product design. This is where I like to connect them: a promise someone can actually see in the product.

Which part of your first-use experience needs a better explanation?

post:2026-10-14.text:
I'm looking for founding designer opportunities and building a consulting practice around product design and brand strategy.

I've worked across creative direction, product design, startup founding, and brand strategy. I want to bring that mix to early teams while there's still room to question the brief.

The first conversation I'd want to have is about the customer. What are they trying to do? Where are they getting stuck? What does the team already know, and what are we guessing?

A rough prototype can give that conversation something concrete. Walk through it together and notice where you disagree. Those moments can tell you what to test next.

If you're looking for a founding designer or considering outside design help, tell me which product decision your team is wrestling with. We can start there.

comment:030fc9ac4fe99e041f5972259fce9f92.text: An early team could compare two prototypes on the same customer task. If a tool speeds up production but leaves the same confusion in the experience, the gain is mostly in throughput. The stronger signal is a clearer decision about what to build.

comment:4c4b90308844974f4b5cfe896d6cd427.text: Satya's focus on reinventing systems of record rather than layering new experiences highlights a strategic shift in product design—prioritizing foundational change that empowers businesses to orchestrate work more effectively. This vision aligns with the need for early-stage teams to rethink design priorities beyond surface-level improvements.

post:2026-10-10:0900.text:
Before opening Figma, write down what someone came to this screen to do.

Say it's an invoice dashboard. A customer opens it because they need to find an unpaid invoice and send a reminder. Can they spot that invoice, understand its status, and send it without hunting through menus?

That's a useful design review. "Make the dashboard cleaner" gives everyone a different problem to solve.

I'd follow the task through the screen once and note each moment that needs explaining. Maybe the status label is vague. Maybe the reminder action is buried. Fix those before spending another afternoon on the card layout.

The visual details still matter. Choosing them gets easier when the team agrees on the task the screen needs to help with.

post:2026-10-10:1800.text:
If you're hiring your first designer, let them into the conversation before the feature list is settled.

Give them the customer calls. Show them the support questions. Explain which assumptions are keeping you up at night.

A designer can turn an uncertain idea into a flow that the team can walk through. Sometimes that exposes a missing step. Sometimes it reveals that two features are trying to solve the same problem.

If the brief only arrives after those decisions, you've already limited what the designer can help with.

I'm interested in founding designer roles where that conversation happens early. My background spans product design, creative direction, brand strategy, and startup founding. I'd want to understand what your customers are struggling with before deciding what to draw.

reply:urn:li:share:7514165310896250880:7.text: Placing a single, visible next-step card where users naturally look reduces friction by delivering immediate value. Tooltips rarely engage, creating a gap between intent and action. This design prioritizes clarity over guidance, ensuring users see a clear path forward without cognitive load.

comment:4385b0b72b60927527e248b98e48ba38.text: Relying solely on data risks filtering out the nuanced, emotional signals users express in real time. Designers must protect moments of unfiltered interaction—like spontaneous conversations or observational notes—to preserve the human context behind product needs.

comment:27b157d624ada88646f61067c9b26ddd.text: The tension between tool proficiency and product quality is central. As AI tools evolve, teams may optimize for speed and system complexity rather than user value. A key trade-off: faster iteration risks shallow impact if not grounded in deep customer understanding and iterative validation.

post:2026-10-11:0900.text:
Counting onboarding screens won't tell you whether someone is ready to use the product.

I'd check what a new customer can do after each step. After entering company details, can they create the thing they signed up to make? After inviting a teammate, do they know what that person can access?

A short setup flow can still leave people confused. A longer one may be useful if every step helps them finish a task.

For the next review, I'd follow one customer goal through setup and write down where progress stops. Maybe the question needs an example. Maybe the next action is unclear. That gives the team a specific change to test.

post:2026-10-11:1800.text:
A founder and a designer can hear the same customer call and come away with different problems to solve.

The founder might hear a request for a missing feature. The designer might notice that the customer couldn't find something already in the product.

I'd want both of those observations in the discussion before anyone commits to a solution. Ask the customer to walk through what they were trying to do. Watch where they get stuck. Then compare that with what each person thought the problem was.

The designer can lead the session while the founder listens and asks follow-ups. Afterwards, agree on what you actually heard and which questions still need testing.

At an early startup, those conversations belong in the same room as product decisions.

comment:269213f1acb8aa5dece48be3ada01af3.text: The idea that work will change radically is obvious, but what’s less clear is how quickly or how deeply. I’d ask: what’s one team process you’re still testing that might shift the most in the next year?

post:2026-10-12:0900.text:
Translating a brand promise into your product means more than just words on a page. It shapes how the interface behaves, the language it uses, and even how support interacts with customers. For example, if your brand promises simplicity, your interface should avoid clutter and guide users clearly through tasks. The language should be straightforward, avoiding jargon, and support should respond with patience and clarity.

For founders, a practical step is to review the product experience through the lens of your brand promise. Ask: Does every interaction reflect what we say we stand for? This can be as simple as running a brand-review prompt during product sprints, checking if the UI, messaging, and support align. That review helps catch disconnects early, so your product feels consistent and trustworthy from the first touch.

comment:785efb4d2a1d4ce389a6db8fb1b0a407.text: The 7x faster Inbox rewrite is impressive. How did you test if it actually improves user task completion, not just speed?

comment:ccfcfc9da5ca61168ca804cb8a104052.text: Fin delivering an instant perfect experience for Anthropic suggests a strong focus on real-time responsiveness. How do they ensure consistency across user interactions without relying on pre-built workflows?

comment:3aa89ae1b93123ae5d817e569b2fcc48.text: Hit Zero today by clearing your inbox for 24 hours. I’d test it with just one priority task: respond to a key customer message. See how the flow changes without email noise.

comment:ef3792f1c612e022bfdafbcba230154d.text: The question about AI reshaping product design is broad. What if we started with a specific user task? For example, how does AI affect the first step of onboarding a new customer? That might reveal more than a general conversation.

comment:54e7b83c1d842b31d3280a20bc85b21b.text: Built a static site in 30 minutes using Codex and S3. That’s fast, but how does it compare to the original design workflow in terms of user experience? I’d test if the new setup loads faster or feels more intuitive on mobile.

It emphasizes the importance of clarity in the user journey, especially between onboarding and the dashboard, where users must grasp the next steps and their value. This focus aligns well with early-stage founders and product leaders who are often refining their product's core user experience and prioritizing design decisions that drive user activation. The practical approach of tracking user tasks and pinpointing where explanations are needed offers a concrete method for founder-designer collaboration, resonating with the audience's interest in design priorities for early-stage teams and working with founding designers. The comment by Tushar Negi, a product designer experienced in SaaS and design systems, reinforces this by highlighting the common gap after sign-up and suggesting design solutions that integrate guidance into the layout rather than relying on overlooked tooltips. While company sizes remain unknown, the content’s relevance to product design and brand strategy in product experiences makes it a good fit for the intended audience. Overall, the post and engagement reflect a thoughtful discussion on practical product design challenges faced by early-stage teams and founders.

targets.text:
Linear CEO, Karri Saarinen: "I took a break this summer from paying attention to AI. I thought that when I came back, I'd feel left behind. But when I came back, I realized that nothing has really changed.

There's new models, there's new techniques, there's new agents. But in the end, making great products, increasing revenue, and building the business—it's still hard. 

It's clear the tools are getting better, you can do more, you can do it faster. But I think the more important question is: are we actually making better things with these tools? Are our teams getting better with these tools? 

I don't think that answer is clearly yes. 

There's a lot of emphasis now on toolmaking and using tools and building systems. But I think in the end, as product people, our job is to make something great."
